The Stanford Prison Experiment. In 1971, Philip Zimbardo conducted an experiment in the basement of Stanford's psychology building that became one of the most controversial studies in psychology history. College students were randomly assigned to play either prisoners or guards in a mock prison. Within days, the experiment descended into psychological abuse and trauma, and Zimbardo concluded that situations, not personalities, drive evil behaviour.

Twenty-four male undergraduates participated, all screened for psychological health beforehand. Guards were given uniforms, dark sunglasses, and billy clubs; prisoners wore smocks and chains and were subjected to dehumanizing procedures including strip searches and being identified only by number. The stage was set for chaos.

Within days, guards engaged in psychological abuse, humiliation, and arbitrary punishment. Prisoners became compliant, depressed, and emotionally broken. One prisoner had a mental breakdown and had to be released. Another led a rebellion that guards violently suppressed. Others became passive and dependent, accepting the degradation as normal.

Zimbardo had planned a two-week study, but he halted it after just six days. A graduate student named Christina Maslach witnessed what was happening and challenged the ethicality of what she saw. When Zimbardo heard her concerns, he stopped the experiment.

From these six days of chaos, Zimbardo drew a sweeping conclusion: ordinary people become perpetrators of abuse when placed in dehumanizing roles, even without any prior inclination toward cruelty. The situation itself corrupted them. He called this the Lucifer Effect—the idea that situations can transform good people into perpetrators.

Yet in recent decades, the study has faced serious methodological critiques. Archival evidence suggests Zimbardo himself may have influenced outcomes, and replication attempts have failed. The Stanford Prison Experiment remains iconic as a story about situational power, but its scientific foundations have proven weaker than its reputation.
